evidence.claim: Northup was a free-born African American farmer and professional violinist from New York.
evidence.quote: Solomon Northup, a free-born African American farmer and professional violinist from New York.

evidence.claim: An offer of traveling musical work took him to Washington in 1841, where he was kidnapped and sold into slavery.
evidence.quote: In 1841, he was offered a traveling musician’s job and was convinced to travel to Washington D.C., where slavery was legal. While there, he was kidnapped and sold into slavery.

evidence.claim: He remained enslaved in central Louisiana until 1853, then returned to New York and wrote Twelve Years a Slave.
evidence.quote: In New Orleans, Northup was given the name “Platt” and eventually arrived in Central Louisiana where he remained a slave from 1841-1853.

evidence.claim: then returned to New York and wrote Twelve Years a Slave.
evidence.quote: Upon his return to New York, Northup chronicled his life as a slave in his memoirs, Twelve Years a Slave

evidence.claim: Later, researchers Sue Eakin and Joseph Logsdon checked the people and events in his memoir and published an annotated edition in 1968.
evidence.quote: Sue Eakin and Joseph Logsdon researched the facts from Northup's book and were able to verify many of the events and people and published their annotated version of the book in 1968.

evidence.claim: Start at Alexandria’s Red River Landing, where Northup disembarked from the steamer Rodolf after being sold in New Orleans.
evidence.quote: the Red River Landing in Alexandria, where Northup and three other slaves disembarked the steamer Rodolf after being sold in New Orleans

evidence.claim: The journey ends in Marksville, where papers recognizing Northup’s freedom were signed at the Avoyelles Parish courthouse in 1853.
evidence.quote: On January 4, 1853 at the Avoyelles Parish Courthouse in Marksville (another site on the trail), papers were signed and Northup was at last a free man again.

evidence.claim: Solomon Northup helped build Edwin Epps’s Creole cottage on Bayou Boeuf in 1852 while Epps held him enslaved.
evidence.quote: Edwin Epps House is a Creole cottage built in 1852 (1852) in part by Solomon Northup on Bayou Boeuf near Holmesville in Avoyelles Parish, Louisiana. It was built for Edwin Epps, a slaveholder.

evidence.claim: while Epps held him enslaved.
evidence.quote: From 1843 to 1853, Epps, a small planter, owned Solomon Northup

evidence.claim: During that year, Northup confided in Canadian carpenter Samuel Bass, who sent letters seeking help from New York.
evidence.quote: In 1852, itinerant Canadian carpenter Samuel Bass came to do some work for Epps.

evidence.claim: Northup confided in Canadian carpenter Samuel Bass, who sent letters seeking help from New York.
evidence.quote: where he met and confided in a Canadian-born carpenter Samuel Bass. Bass is credited with writing several letters on Northup’s behalf to friends and officials in New York in hopes of finding help.

evidence.claim: The house has since moved twice: to Bunkie in 1976, then to LSU Alexandria in 1999.
evidence.quote: The house was relocated twice. In 1976, it was moved to nearby Bunkie.

evidence.claim: At the second move it was dismantled and reconstructed, with some original materials replaced.
evidence.quote: In 1999, the house was dismantled, during which some original building materials were replaced, and reconstructed on the Louisiana State University of Alexandria.

evidence.claim: A room is dedicated to Northup’s story.
evidence.quote: There is a room in the house that is dedicated to telling Northup's story.

evidence.claim: Historian Sue Eakin located the house while investigating the accuracy of Northup’s memoir, connecting his written testimony to the building he helped construct.
evidence.quote: As part of the research, she found the house that Northup built, the Edwin Epps House.

evidence.claim: William Prince Ford links Cheneyville’s religious history to Northup’s enslavement.
evidence.quote: Ford is also known as the original enslaver of Solomon Northup

evidence.claim: Ford bought Northup in New Orleans in 1841, after Northup had been kidnapped in Washington.
evidence.quote: Northup was an African-American who had been born free, but kidnapped in Washington, D.C., and sold to Ford in New Orleans in 1841.

evidence.claim: Two years later, influenced by Alexander Campbell’s writings, Ford led most of a Baptist congregation into the Church of Christ.
evidence.quote: In 1843 most of the membership of a Baptist congregation, under the leadership of William Prince Ford, who had been influenced by Campbell's writings, became a Church of Christ.

evidence.claim: The Cheneyville Christian Church is Louisiana’s oldest congregation associated with the Restoration Movement.
evidence.quote: The Cheneyville Christian Church is the oldest congregation associated with the Restoration Movement in Louisiana.
